Executive Summary
Our project is to design an electrically propelled, remote-controlled boat to compete in the Promoting
Electric Propulsion 2025 competition. This competition seeks innovations in electric technologies for use
in the military and industrial sectors. Our team’s key goals are to design, fabricate, and test an uncrewed
electric boat from the ground up. The University of Alabama competed in PEP 24, coming in first place in
the uncrewed boat division. We intend to continue this streak of excellence in PEP 25 by scoring well on
our white paper assignment and video presentation and performing well on race day. Our boat will be a
deep V-monohull optimized for planing. We will propel our boat with two propellers powered by two 4.5
kW motors with an open-loop cooling system. We designed our boat hull in SolidWorks and used Ansys to
calculate the drag force and optimize the deadrise angle.
We will test our motors using a test rig that can measure the heat generation and torque outputs to
effectively cool our system and understand better how our boat should perform. We plan to fabricate the
hull out of fiberglass and glue it together with epoxy. Our budget of $8,000 has been mainly allocated
towards the hull fabrication and the propulsion systems. We are seeking sponsorship from the university to
fund our travel costs. After finishing the design of our boat, we will extensively test it in Lake Tuscaloosa
to gauge its performance and the duration of the battery life, making corrections as necessary. Our robust
hull design will provide lift through the 17-degree deadrise angle and the presence of strakes, enabling it to
plane sooner and minimize drag. Our team faced several challenges in the design of our vessel, such as
learning how to design boats (which lack governing equations or universal design guidelines), learning
unfamiliar software, learning how to lay fiberglass properly, balancing the battery requirements while
minimizing weight, and innovating our fabrication processes when faced with insufficient supplies. The
project has taught our team the importance of cross-team collaboration, forcing us to communicate
effectively between each other to solve the problems at hand, and to go outside of ourselves to learn from 4

experts in fields such as boat design and control components. We highly appreciate our client, Dr. Briscoe,
who has given us welcome guidance as we navigate this project. Our team is prepared for the coming tasks,
and because of our excellent team synergy, we will adapt to any challenges that might arise in the final
stretch of our project.5

Project Objectives/Scope
The University of Alabama PEP team will compete in the unmanned division this year. The team will
be tasked with designing and fabricating an unmanned vessel for use in the competition in April 2025.
The design is subject to several constraints, which are discussed further in the design requirements
section. The student-led nature of the project means that the scope of the competition encompasses initial
design, prototyping, fabrication, testing, and parts sourcing for the final product.
1. Design
a. Hull: CAD and CFD programs will be used to design an optimal hull for the conditions
and objectives of the PEP competition.
b. Power System: Based on motors and propellers used, a power storage system in the form
of a battery pack will be properly sized and integrated into the boat.
c. Controls System: A controls system will be sourced and developed such that the boat can
be reliably controlled throughout the duration of the race.
2. Prototyping
a. Hull: Scale models of the chosen design will be constructed to test performance and give
the team fiberglass fabrication experience.
b. Power System: The appropriate motors will be tested with the complete battery pack to
ensure operation and identify potential issues, such as heat generation.
3. Fabrication
a. Hull: The team will determine an appropriate fabrication method and fabricate the hull
from scratch using university facilities and sourced materials.
b. Power Systems: Battery pack and management system will be constructed using 3D
printed parts, a spot welder, and soldered components. 7

4. Material Sourcing
a. Within the given budget of $8,000, the team will source all materials and components
necessary to build a functioning boat before the competition date in April.
5. Competition
a. The team will pilot the completed boat remotely during the 2-mile race from April 15th to
17th.
The objective of this project is to design, fabricate, and compete with a high-performance unmanned
vessel in the ASNE PEP25 competition. The team will optimize the hull design using CAD and CFD
software to ensure efficiency, speed, and stability under race conditions. A reliable power system will be
engineered by selecting appropriate motors, propellers, and a properly sized battery pack to sustain
operation throughout the competition. Additionally, a robust control system will be developed to enable
stable and responsive remote operation, ensuring precise maneuverability and compliance with
competition requirements. To validate the design, scale models of the hull and power system will be
prototyped and tested for performance, durability, and manufacturability before final fabrication. The fullscale vessel will be constructed using appropriate materials and fabrication techniques, integrating all
components into a cohesive system. All materials and components will be sourced within the allocated
$8,000 budget while maintaining quality and performance standards. Ultimately, the goal is to ensure the
vessel is fully functional, meets all competition regulations, and is ready for remote piloting in the 2-mile
endurance race in April 2025.8

Technical Approach
Hull Team
Much research and discussion has gone into designing a new hull for this competition, making
note of last year’s setbacks to avoid a similar situation. Due to the manufacturability constraint of no team
member having extensive manufacturing experience, we felt that a monohull design would be the best
decision for our needs. An emphasis was put on ensuring the boat is lightweight, can achieve planing
quickly, and has a low drag on the water. Fiberglass was used to construct the hull, and plywood stringers
to fill out the frame on the inside to ensure the boat is lightweight. The fiberglass operation consisted of
three main parts: create a foam plug, create a female fiberglass mold, then layup the boat and stringers.
After these steps were executed, a top deck was then attached and fiber glassed, along with a latch for
easy access to the boat internals. The final step for the hull was to carefully drill holes for the shafts,
tubes, and external assemblies, ensuring that they are properly sealed with marine sealer.
The next key design consideration for the boat hull is its ability to plane and cut through the water.
A boat that can easily plane and is sharp through the water will require less power to drive, removing
some burden on the power requirements. Much research was done by reading books on boat design,
talking with industry experts, and using ANSYS to optimize our boat geometry to achieve the desired
results. Through these resources, the boat’s deadrise, the angle of the bottom of the boat from the
horizontal, was chosen to be 17 degrees. A 17-degree deadrise is the sweet spot for planing and waveslicing capability.
One of the critical requirements for this year’s race is that unmanned boats must carry 30 or 60
lbs. for bonus points. The new hull design must handle a 60 lb. load and perform swiftly in the water. For
this reason, the boat has been lengthened and widened compared to last year’s design. The new hull will 9

be 7.5 feet long, 28 inches wide, and 10 inches deep. These dimensions will allow the boat to easily
handle up to 160 lbs., which will also allow larger motors and batteries to be used. Our goal is to produce
a high quality boat while staying within the economic constraints given to us by ASNE.
Controls Team
Utilizing PEP24’s ideas as a foundation for a layout, a systems diagram was generated to house all
the electronics and propulsion systems within the boat. This vessel will only be moved by electric
propulsion, promoting an emission-free boat. This diagram shows the setup for the boat’s internals.
Figure (1). Systems Diagram
From Figure (1), the main battery provides power solely to the motors for maximum propulsion
capabilities controlled through the ESC’s. We are using a six-channel RadioMaster PWM receiver with a
RadioMaster radio controller (ELRS programmed) to control the boat. This receiver is responsible for 10

sending signals for a set of pumps, two servos, and two ESC’s. Beginning with the motors, we calculated
the required power rating of the motors to maintain our wanted speeds of 35-40 mph to be 4.5 KW each.
We will be utilizing the Series 5684 1050 KV motor that has a max amp draw of 165 Amps. These motors
are directly connected to the propeller via straight 8 mm shaft providing a 1:1 power transfer. Because of
heating limitations, we will run the motors at about 100 amps each. From proper consideration of short
time running and power draw, we decided that 10-gauge wire is sufficient to handle our needs. This
wiring should be sufficient to handle the amperage. In terms of the ESC, we want to make sure the ESC
can handle the max amp draw the motor is capable of for user safety and handling. We are using the ZTW
180 burst amp draw ESC with a 10 A battery eliminator circuit (BEC). This BEC will provide adequate
power to the servos and receiver at a selectable voltage from 5-8.4 V. We will be emulating a traditional
RC boat turning system, using 45 KG servos to turn our rudders. As the dynamics of the boat will vary
with speed, center of mass, and turbulence, we opted to go for a super conservative value of 45 KG of
torque; which is higher than last year’s boat. From PEP 24, the major issue in the system was their
cooling system. This year we will utilize a revamped cooling system with bigger pumps to ensure
adequate heat transfer.11

Figure (2). Cooling System Diagram
We are using 2 C1EC circulating pumps for this operation. These bigger pumps will pull enough
flow mass flow rate to carry heat out of our system. Both pumps will run separate loops throughout the
boat to provide cooling to each set of ESC and motor. Originally, the ESC we bought was designed for air
cooling. Since our boat is an enclosed system, we opted to strip the fan and use thermal paste, thermal
padding, and an aluminum water cooling block to provide immense conductive heat transfer.
Unfortunately, each of these pumps require 12 volts 1.2 amps for operation. However, due to PEP 25
guidelines, we are granted an additional battery for the control systems independent of the battery used for
the motors which is shown in Figure (1) through the red lines. These pumps will be controlled by a single
switch relay as shown in Figure (1) to power the pumps only when needed for power conservation. Using
our radiomaster controller, we will implement kill switches (using the relay) to our pumps and even a
throttle cut to both of our motors for safety. Finally, two high amperage physical kill switches will be
installed on top of the boat to kill power to both the motors for safety. Moving forward, the 3D printed 12

rudders will provide water inlets to allow the pumps to have a water source. Each fin has a surface area of
16in2, and there are two of them, providing ample amount of turning for the boat. One interesting note on
the rudders is the material used to print them. For good properties in water, PETG was used instead of
PLA. PVA, a water-soluble plastic, was used as supports for the fins, which made cleaning off the
supports significantly easier.
Power System
An electric power system must power the boat’s propulsion system to meet the competition’s
design requirements. This power system consists of a power storage unit composed of lithium-ion
batteries, a battery management system, and an electric motor. From research done into the hull design
and effects of drag during operation, it has been determined that two 4.5kW motors will be used as the
primary method of propulsion to meet and exceed the 4kW power requirement needed to obtain a design
speed of 30 knots, as well as to provide redundancy in the event of a failure during the competition. The
chosen motor is a traditional RC motor format due to its ability to operate at incredibly high speeds
compared to its power draw, small size, and optimized design for the application.
This motor system powers a bank of lithium-ion batteries designed to produce between 44.4 and
55.5 volts at maximum current draws of up to 300 amps. This battery system allows the motors to operate
at optimal speed for the duration of the race without exceeding competition voltage requirements or
running out of power during the competition. While fabricating a customized battery pack using smaller
cylindrical cells was considered, the team ultimately decided on utilizing an array of 22.2V 6 Ah LiPo
batteries of the type typically used in RC applications. Two battery banks have been created, one to power
each motor. To achieve the 45V operating voltage of the motors, sets of two batteries were wired together
in series creating an array of two cells with 44.4V of potential and 6 Ah of capacity. To ensure an
operating time of approximately 30 minutes at a peak operating current of 100 amps per motor, six of 13

these arrays per motor were wired in parallel, giving each battery bank 36 Ah of capacity. To achieve this,
series and parallel connectors had to be fabricated using 10 AWG wire the same EC5 connection standard
present on the batteries.
Safety and environmental concerns were also considered heavily in the design of the power
system. The large number of batteries included in parallel configuration not only increases the amount of
available capacity but also allows for lower current draw rates for each individual cell, reducing stress and
thereby the change of thermal runaway and massive heat generation. This not only reduces the safety
hazards of handling and operating the boat but also minimizes the chance of fouling the competition
grounds with hazardous battery material in the event of failure. It was also decided that the battery system
will be cooled via a similar system to the motor cooling to further reduced the risk of thermal runaway,
but also to ensure that the battery compartment can be sealed to prevent leakage and damage to the cells
as well as the risk of environmental contamination in the event of a failure. It is also important to note that
by building an electric power boat, we will be helping to reduce the emissions released by the more
common gasoline-powered boats. By promoting electric propulsion, ASNE is working to build a
community that is more economically and environmentally friendly.
Propulsion
It was decided from the beginning of this project that the boat would utilize two propellers. Not
only does this design have superior maneuverability and fuel efficiency over a single propeller design, it
also brings a level of redundancy into the system. If one motor fails (either by overheating which occurred
in the previous competition or by power supply issues), there would still be one motor/propeller system
driving the boat forward, albeit slower. In the dual propeller design, the propellers rotate in opposite
directions, as shown in Figure (3). This counter-rotation eliminates any unwanted torques from being
applied to the hull (which could cause tipping) and it also eliminates the phenomenon of “prop walk” 14

wherein a propeller pushes the back of the boat to starboard or port side causing an unintentional turn of
direction. Additionally, due to the complexity that arises from installing a gearbox, it was also determined
that the propellers would be directly connected to the motors (and thus have a 1:1 rotation ratio with the
motors).
Figure (3). Diagram of Propeller Rotation
From preliminary simulations of the boat in Ansys, drag values were defined for multiple speeds,
as summarized in Table (1). These drag values correlate to the minimum required thrusts that the
propellers must achieve so that the boat will move forward. From the motor specifications, it is also
known that the stall torque is 1.5 Nm and the no load speed is 46,620 rpm with an applied voltage of 44.4
V as with our power system. With these parameters, a motor performance curve can be constructed,
shown in Figure (4), wherein all points that lie below this curve are achievable torque/speed
combinations.15

Four cases of changing pitch-to-diameter ratio (P/D) values were examined in the open water

(because n is very high) and torque will be a limiting factor. Thus, P/D was set to a value of 0.5. 17

Similarly, the open water performance curve were used to test 4 cases of varying blade aero ratio
(AE/AO). Low AE/AO values have greater CT and CQ values at low advance ratios, however, at high
advance ratios they have lower CT and CQ values. The converse is also true for high AE/AO values. Thus,
to limit CQ at the low advance ratios we operate at, the AE/AO value was set to 0.3.18

To manufacture this design, the propellers first had to be modeled in CAD. OpenVSP was used to
model the complex geometry of the blades as this software is particularly adept at modeling designs that
prioritize fluid dynamics. The blades were then imported into SolidWorks and the hub and shaft coupler
connection were modeled. Prototypes were made in PLA before investing in prints with better material
characteristics. There are two sets of final propellers, one made of Tough 1500 resin and one 3D printed
with a carbon fiber reinforced nylon composite, shown in Figure (9). These propellers were sanded and
had a layer of epoxy and fiberglass applied to reinforce the hub-blade connections which were the failure 19

points in earlier prototype testing. Having two sets of propellers allows the team to test the material limits
of the propulsion system.

Evaluation Method
To gauge the performance, longevity, and heat generation characteristics of our power train
design, a test rig was designed to replicate the real-world operation of the drive system. This testing
system allows the batteries and motors to be examined in isolation at different operating conditions to
guide the team’s decision regarding cooling system design and adding additional energy storage to
increase runtime.
Test Rig Design
The first test measured the thrust generated by our propellers and assessed heat production. We
used a strain gauge on a cantilever beam positioned at a 90-degree angle to the motor to capture the data.
Four thermocouples were used to monitor the temperature of each component, with one placed on the flat
side of the battery pack being examined and one placed on the long end next to the wire connections and
charging balancer. The third was placed on or adjacent to the electronic speed controller and the final one
will be affixed to the outer casing of the motor. These thermocouples were used to record the temperature
of each device over the course of the experiment. The test concluded a successful trial of the setup with
the propeller able to sustain loads up to 17000 rpm. At this speed, the ESC was showing considerable
amounts of amperage draw, which was expected. The ESC, however, sustained a high temperature of 90
degrees Celsius. This, however, will be remedied by our method of thermal paste to allow for more
contact area of heat transfer.
To test the failure mechanisms of different powertrain systems, a test setup was created to simulate
a worst-case scenario load on the powertrain components. The setup consisted of a wooden stand to
mount the motor, pump, and control systems on, as well as a board running parallel to the shaft to allow
for shaft support. The heat of the speed controllers, motor RPM, current draw, and throttle percentage 21

were monitored through the ZTW app. For some testing, thrust was determined by attaching the motor to
a steel beam of known quantity outfitted with a strain gauge, whose values were recorded for thrust
calculation. The test took place in a pool of ample depth and length to avoid the effects of turbulence in
the water.
During the performance test, two cells were wired in series and operated at the current that would
be expected of an individual 44.4V cell under craft operation, approximately 20 amps. The throttle
position was increased slowly until reaching a motor speed of approximately 20,000 RPM and the readout
for all data listed above was recorded to be able to collect data over time. At the maximum RPM reached,
the vibration of the shaft was deemed too significant, and the test was concluded.
The test was then repeated after allowing the power components ample time to cool, but this time
throttle was increased at a slower rate to gauge the thermal performance. At time of testing, inadequate
thermal contact was made between the ESC and associated water block. The testing was performed as a
worst-case scenario in terms of thermal contact, and the thermal contact issues have since been remedied.
At time of testing, the motor was able to maintain 15% throttle for approximately 90 seconds before the
thermal limits of the equipment were reached. Corrective measures were taken to ensure better thermal
contact between heat generating components and water block.
The test illustrated the durability of the materials used in the propellers and shaft, demonstrating
that these would likely not be points of failure under operation. Additionally, the ability of the power
system to perform for an extended period without overheating with inadequate cooling bolstered
confidence in the effectiveness of the cooling system as it stands. Additionally, the strain data gained
during the test allowed a thrust to throttle percentage curve to be determined, allowing the potential thrust
of the system at different currents to be estimated. The height of the test rig was also varied during 22

operation to mitigate propeller cavitation, giving valuable insight into the height at which the propellers
should be mounted relative to the surface of the water.
These tests will be repeated following the retrofitting of the power system with more robust
components, including cast aluminum propellers and a more rigorous thermal management system. Future
testing will take place with the propulsion system fully packaged inside the finished boat to determine the
boat’s dynamic properties, as well as to determine the limits to be set in the control system relating to
power delivery and calibration. 23

Risks
During the design and build process, we identified and mitigated key risks to enhance the
reliability and performance of our unmanned vessel. To address potential overheating—an issue that
challenged last year’s team—we developed a robust cooling system incorporating two pumps to actively
cool the electronic speed controllers (ESCs) and motors. Additionally, we applied thermal paste and
installed a cooling block along the ESCs for improved heat dissipation. If overheating persists during
testing, we have contingency plans, including integrating a cooled payload to maintain a lower internal
temperature during the race. To prevent structural failures, we conducted multiple leak tests and
reinforced high-risk areas—primarily in the rear of the vessel—with additional material layers. These
areas were patched, tested, and sealed for durability. Weight was a critical design consideration; we used
SolidWorks to estimate total mass and ANSYS simulations to validate the vessel’s structural integrity
under load conditions. To mitigate battery failure risks, we procured extra batteries and implemented a
structured charging schedule leading up to the race. We also maximized the number of parallel battery
connections to reduce current draw per cell, enhancing overall power efficiency. Additionally, to protect
the vessel during transit, we invested in a trailer and constructed a custom stand for secure transportation.
As race day approaches, we will continue monitoring heat levels, battery performance, and
structural integrity in real time, ensuring optimal performance while proactively addressing emerging
risks.24

Executive Summary
Our project is to design an electrically propelled, remote-controlled boat to compete in the Promoting
Electric Propulsion 2025 competition. This competition seeks innovations in electric technologies for use
in the military and industrial sectors. Our team’s key goals are to design, fabricate, and test an uncrewed
electric boat from the ground up. The University of Alabama competed in PEP 24, coming in first place in
the uncrewed boat division. We intend to continue this streak of excellence in PEP 25 by scoring well on
our white paper assignment and video presentation and performing well on race day. Our boat will be a
deep V-monohull optimized for planing. We will propel our boat with two propellers powered by two 4.5
kW motors with an open-loop cooling system. We designed our boat hull in SolidWorks and used Ansys to
calculate the drag force and optimize the deadrise angle.
We will test our motors using a test rig that can measure the heat generation and torque outputs to
effectively cool our system and understand better how our boat should perform. We plan to fabricate the
hull out of fiberglass and glue it together with epoxy. Our budget of $8,000 has been mainly allocated
towards the hull fabrication and the propulsion systems. We are seeking sponsorship from the university to
fund our travel costs. After finishing the design of our boat, we will extensively test it in Lake Tuscaloosa
to gauge its performance and the duration of the battery life, making corrections as necessary. Our robust
hull design will provide lift through the 17-degree deadrise angle and the presence of strakes, enabling it to
plane sooner and minimize drag. Our team faced several challenges in the design of our vessel, such as
learning how to design boats (which lack governing equations or universal design guidelines), learning
unfamiliar software, learning how to lay fiberglass properly, balancing the battery requirements while
minimizing weight, and innovating our fabrication processes when faced with insufficient supplies. The
project has taught our team the importance of cross-team collaboration, forcing us to communicate
effectively between each other to solve the problems at hand, and to go outside of ourselves to learn from 4
experts in fields such as boat design and control components. We highly appreciate our client, Dr. Briscoe,
who has given us welcome guidance as we navigate this project. Our team is prepared for the coming tasks,
and because of our excellent team synergy, we will adapt to any challenges that might arise in the final
stretch of our project.5
Table of Contents
Project Objectives/Scope
The University of Alabama PEP team will compete in the unmanned division this year. The team will
be tasked with designing and fabricating an unmanned vessel for use in the competition in April 2025.
The design is subject to several constraints, which are discussed further in the design requirements
section. The student-led nature of the project means that the scope of the competition encompasses initial
design, prototyping, fabrication, testing, and parts sourcing for the final product.
1. Design
a. Hull: CAD and CFD programs will be used to design an optimal hull for the conditions
and objectives of the PEP competition.
b. Power System: Based on motors and propellers used, a power storage system in the form
of a battery pack will be properly sized and integrated into the boat.
c. Controls System: A controls system will be sourced and developed such that the boat can
be reliably controlled throughout the duration of the race.
2. Prototyping
a. Hull: Scale models of the chosen design will be constructed to test performance and give
the team fiberglass fabrication experience.
b. Power System: The appropriate motors will be tested with the complete battery pack to
ensure operation and identify potential issues, such as heat generation.
3. Fabrication
a. Hull: The team will determine an appropriate fabrication method and fabricate the hull
from scratch using university facilities and sourced materials.
b. Power Systems: Battery pack and management system will be constructed using 3D
printed parts, a spot welder, and soldered components. 7
4. Material Sourcing
a. Within the given budget of $8,000, the team will source all materials and components
necessary to build a functioning boat before the competition date in April.
5. Competition
a. The team will pilot the completed boat remotely during the 2-mile race from April 15th to
17th.
The objective of this project is to design, fabricate, and compete with a high-performance unmanned
vessel in the ASNE PEP25 competition. The team will optimize the hull design using CAD and CFD
software to ensure efficiency, speed, and stability under race conditions. A reliable power system will be
engineered by selecting appropriate motors, propellers, and a properly sized battery pack to sustain
operation throughout the competition. Additionally, a robust control system will be developed to enable
stable and responsive remote operation, ensuring precise maneuverability and compliance with
competition requirements. To validate the design, scale models of the hull and power system will be

prototyped and tested for performance, durability, and manufacturability before final fabrication. The fullscale vessel will be constructed using appropriate materials and fabrication techniques, integrating all
components into a cohesive system. All materials and components will be sourced within the allocated
$8,000 budget while maintaining quality and performance standards. Ultimately, the goal is to ensure the
vessel is fully functional, meets all competition regulations, and is ready for remote piloting in the 2-mile
endurance race in April 2025.8
Technical Approach
Hull Team
Much research and discussion has gone into designing a new hull for this competition, making
note of last year’s setbacks to avoid a similar situation. Due to the manufacturability constraint of no team
member having extensive manufacturing experience, we felt that a monohull design would be the best
decision for our needs. An emphasis was put on ensuring the boat is lightweight, can achieve planing
quickly, and has a low drag on the water. Fiberglass was used to construct the hull, and plywood stringers
to fill out the frame on the inside to ensure the boat is lightweight. The fiberglass operation consisted of
three main parts: create a foam plug, create a female fiberglass mold, then layup the boat and stringers.
After these steps were executed, a top deck was then attached and fiber glassed, along with a latch for
easy access to the boat internals. The final step for the hull was to carefully drill holes for the shafts,
tubes, and external assemblies, ensuring that they are properly sealed with marine sealer.
The next key design consideration for the boat hull is its ability to plane and cut through the water.
A boat that can easily plane and is sharp through the water will require less power to drive, removing
some burden on the power requirements. Much research was done by reading books on boat design,
talking with industry experts, and using ANSYS to optimize our boat geometry to achieve the desired
results. Through these resources, the boat’s deadrise, the angle of the bottom of the boat from the
horizontal, was chosen to be 17 degrees. A 17-degree deadrise is the sweet spot for planing and waveslicing capability.
One of the critical requirements for this year’s race is that unmanned boats must carry 30 or 60
lbs. for bonus points. The new hull design must handle a 60 lb. load and perform swiftly in the water. For
this reason, the boat has been lengthened and widened compared to last year’s design. The new hull will 9
be 7.5 feet long, 28 inches wide, and 10 inches deep. These dimensions will allow the boat to easily
handle up to 160 lbs., which will also allow larger motors and batteries to be used. Our goal is to produce
a high quality boat while staying within the economic constraints given to us by ASNE.
Controls Team
Utilizing PEP24’s ideas as a foundation for a layout, a systems diagram was generated to house all
the electronics and propulsion systems within the boat. This vessel will only be moved by electric
propulsion, promoting an emission-free boat. This diagram shows the setup for the boat’s internals.
Figure (1). Systems Diagram
From Figure (1), the main battery provides power solely to the motors for maximum propulsion
capabilities controlled through the ESC’s. We are using a six-channel RadioMaster PWM receiver with a
RadioMaster radio controller (ELRS programmed) to control the boat. This receiver is responsible for 10
sending signals for a set of pumps, two servos, and two ESC’s. Beginning with the motors, we calculated
the required power rating of the motors to maintain our wanted speeds of 35-40 mph to be 4.5 KW each.
We will be utilizing the Series 5684 1050 KV motor that has a max amp draw of 165 Amps. These motors
are directly connected to the propeller via straight 8 mm shaft providing a 1:1 power transfer. Because of
heating limitations, we will run the motors at about 100 amps each. From proper consideration of short
time running and power draw, we decided that 10-gauge wire is sufficient to handle our needs. This
wiring should be sufficient to handle the amperage. In terms of the ESC, we want to make sure the ESC
can handle the max amp draw the motor is capable of for user safety and handling. We are using the ZTW
180 burst amp draw ESC with a 10 A battery eliminator circuit (BEC). This BEC will provide adequate
power to the servos and receiver at a selectable voltage from 5-8.4 V. We will be emulating a traditional
RC boat turning system, using 45 KG servos to turn our rudders. As the dynamics of the boat will vary
with speed, center of mass, and turbulence, we opted to go for a super conservative value of 45 KG of
torque; which is higher than last year’s boat. From PEP 24, the major issue in the system was their
cooling system. This year we will utilize a revamped cooling system with bigger pumps to ensure
adequate heat transfer.11
Figure (2). Cooling System Diagram
We are using 2 C1EC circulating pumps for this operation. These bigger pumps will pull enough
flow mass flow rate to carry heat out of our system. Both pumps will run separate loops throughout the
boat to provide cooling to each set of ESC and motor. Originally, the ESC we bought was designed for air
cooling. Since our boat is an enclosed system, we opted to strip the fan and use thermal paste, thermal
padding, and an aluminum water cooling block to provide immense conductive heat transfer.
Unfortunately, each of these pumps require 12 volts 1.2 amps for operation. However, due to PEP 25
guidelines, we are granted an additional battery for the control systems independent of the battery used for
the motors which is shown in Figure (1) through the red lines. These pumps will be controlled by a single
switch relay as shown in Figure (1) to power the pumps only when needed for power conservation. Using
our radiomaster controller, we will implement kill switches (using the relay) to our pumps and even a
throttle cut to both of our motors for safety. Finally, two high amperage physical kill switches will be
installed on top of the boat to kill power to both the motors for safety. Moving forward, the 3D printed 12
rudders will provide water inlets to allow the pumps to have a water source. Each fin has a surface area of
16in2, and there are two of them, providing ample amount of turning for the boat. One interesting note on
the rudders is the material used to print them. For good properties in water, PETG was used instead of
PLA. PVA, a water-soluble plastic, was used as supports for the fins, which made cleaning off the
supports significantly easier.
Power System
An electric power system must power the boat’s propulsion system to meet the competition’s
design requirements. This power system consists of a power storage unit composed of lithium-ion
batteries, a battery management system, and an electric motor. From research done into the hull design
and effects of drag during operation, it has been determined that two 4.5kW motors will be used as the
primary method of propulsion to meet and exceed the 4kW power requirement needed to obtain a design
speed of 30 knots, as well as to provide redundancy in the event of a failure during the competition. The
chosen motor is a traditional RC motor format due to its ability to operate at incredibly high speeds
compared to its power draw, small size, and optimized design for the application.
This motor system powers a bank of lithium-ion batteries designed to produce between 44.4 and
55.5 volts at maximum current draws of up to 300 amps. This battery system allows the motors to operate
at optimal speed for the duration of the race without exceeding competition voltage requirements or
running out of power during the competition. While fabricating a customized battery pack using smaller
cylindrical cells was considered, the team ultimately decided on utilizing an array of 22.2V 6 Ah LiPo
batteries of the type typically used in RC applications. Two battery banks have been created, one to power
each motor. To achieve the 45V operating voltage of the motors, sets of two batteries were wired together
in series creating an array of two cells with 44.4V of potential and 6 Ah of capacity. To ensure an
operating time of approximately 30 minutes at a peak operating current of 100 amps per motor, six of 13
these arrays per motor were wired in parallel, giving each battery bank 36 Ah of capacity. To achieve this,
series and parallel connectors had to be fabricated using 10 AWG wire the same EC5 connection standard
present on the batteries.
Safety and environmental concerns were also considered heavily in the design of the power
system. The large number of batteries included in parallel configuration not only increases the amount of
available capacity but also allows for lower current draw rates for each individual cell, reducing stress and
thereby the change of thermal runaway and massive heat generation. This not only reduces the safety
hazards of handling and operating the boat but also minimizes the chance of fouling the competition
grounds with hazardous battery material in the event of failure. It was also decided that the battery system
will be cooled via a similar system to the motor cooling to further reduced the risk of thermal runaway,
but also to ensure that the battery compartment can be sealed to prevent leakage and damage to the cells
as well as the risk of environmental contamination in the event of a failure. It is also important to note that
by building an electric power boat, we will be helping to reduce the emissions released by the more
common gasoline-powered boats. By promoting electric propulsion, ASNE is working to build a
community that is more economically and environmentally friendly.
Propulsion
It was decided from the beginning of this project that the boat would utilize two propellers. Not
only does this design have superior maneuverability and fuel efficiency over a single propeller design, it
also brings a level of redundancy into the system. If one motor fails (either by overheating which occurred
in the previous competition or by power supply issues), there would still be one motor/propeller system
driving the boat forward, albeit slower. In the dual propeller design, the propellers rotate in opposite
directions, as shown in Figure (3). This counter-rotation eliminates any unwanted torques from being
applied to the hull (which could cause tipping) and it also eliminates the phenomenon of “prop walk” 14
wherein a propeller pushes the back of the boat to starboard or port side causing an unintentional turn of
direction. Additionally, due to the complexity that arises from installing a gearbox, it was also determined
that the propellers would be directly connected to the motors (and thus have a 1:1 rotation ratio with the
motors).
Figure (3). Diagram of Propeller Rotation
From preliminary simulations of the boat in Ansys, drag values were defined for multiple speeds,
as summarized in Table (1). These drag values correlate to the minimum required thrusts that the
propellers must achieve so that the boat will move forward. From the motor specifications, it is also
known that the stall torque is 1.5 Nm and the no load speed is 46,620 rpm with an applied voltage of 44.4
V as with our power system. With these parameters, a motor performance curve can be constructed,
shown in Figure (4), wherein all points that lie below this curve are achievable torque/speed
combinations.15

propeller with a diameter of 3 inches was chosen as the basis for our propeller design. Not only is the Bscrew highly efficient, with its popularity in use, it has many resources on optimization as well as
predicted open-water performance. To further develop the specific geometry of the propellers, the open

curve and drag values to overcome. Prior to this comparison, however, the design requirements outlined
above were converted to the non-dimensional performance characteristics of Advance Ratio (J),

the propeller, Treq is the required thrust, ρ is water density, Fdrag is the drag forces shown in Table (1), and
Qavail is the available motor torque given on the performance curve shown in Figure (4). The results of
these conversions are shown in Figures 5 through 8.
Four cases of changing pitch-to-diameter ratio (P/D) values were examined in the open water
performance curves for a 3-blade b-series propeller and were used to produce the curves shown in Figure
(5) and Figure (6). As P/D increases, both CT and CQ values increase for all advance ratios. Because the

(because n is very high) and torque will be a limiting factor. Thus, P/D was set to a value of 0.5. 17

Similarly, the open water performance curve were used to test 4 cases of varying blade aero ratio
(AE/AO). Low AE/AO values have greater CT and CQ values at low advance ratios, however, at high
advance ratios they have lower CT and CQ values. The converse is also true for high AE/AO values. Thus,
to limit CQ at the low advance ratios we operate at, the AE/AO value was set to 0.3.18

To manufacture this design, the propellers first had to be modeled in CAD. OpenVSP was used to
model the complex geometry of the blades as this software is particularly adept at modeling designs that
prioritize fluid dynamics. The blades were then imported into SolidWorks and the hub and shaft coupler
connection were modeled. Prototypes were made in PLA before investing in prints with better material
characteristics. There are two sets of final propellers, one made of Tough 1500 resin and one 3D printed
with a carbon fiber reinforced nylon composite, shown in Figure (9). These propellers were sanded and
had a layer of epoxy and fiberglass applied to reinforce the hub-blade connections which were the failure 19
points in earlier prototype testing. Having two sets of propellers allows the team to test the material limits
of the propulsion system.
Figure (9): Carbon fiber reinforced nylon composite propeller from (a) shaft perspective and from (b)
downstream perspective and Tough 1500 resin printed propeller from (c) shaft perspective and from (d)
downstream perspective 20
Evaluation Method
To gauge the performance, longevity, and heat generation characteristics of our power train
design, a test rig was designed to replicate the real-world operation of the drive system. This testing
system allows the batteries and motors to be examined in isolation at different operating conditions to
guide the team’s decision regarding cooling system design and adding additional energy storage to
increase runtime.
Test Rig Design
The first test measured the thrust generated by our propellers and assessed heat production. We
used a strain gauge on a cantilever beam positioned at a 90-degree angle to the motor to capture the data.
Four thermocouples were used to monitor the temperature of each component, with one placed on the flat
side of the battery pack being examined and one placed on the long end next to the wire connections and
charging balancer. The third was placed on or adjacent to the electronic speed controller and the final one
will be affixed to the outer casing of the motor. These thermocouples were used to record the temperature
of each device over the course of the experiment. The test concluded a successful trial of the setup with
the propeller able to sustain loads up to 17000 rpm. At this speed, the ESC was showing considerable
amounts of amperage draw, which was expected. The ESC, however, sustained a high temperature of 90
degrees Celsius. This, however, will be remedied by our method of thermal paste to allow for more
contact area of heat transfer.
To test the failure mechanisms of different powertrain systems, a test setup was created to simulate
a worst-case scenario load on the powertrain components. The setup consisted of a wooden stand to
mount the motor, pump, and control systems on, as well as a board running parallel to the shaft to allow
for shaft support. The heat of the speed controllers, motor RPM, current draw, and throttle percentage 21
were monitored through the ZTW app. For some testing, thrust was determined by attaching the motor to
a steel beam of known quantity outfitted with a strain gauge, whose values were recorded for thrust
calculation. The test took place in a pool of ample depth and length to avoid the effects of turbulence in
the water.
During the performance test, two cells were wired in series and operated at the current that would
be expected of an individual 44.4V cell under craft operation, approximately 20 amps. The throttle
position was increased slowly until reaching a motor speed of approximately 20,000 RPM and the readout
for all data listed above was recorded to be able to collect data over time. At the maximum RPM reached,
the vibration of the shaft was deemed too significant, and the test was concluded.
The test was then repeated after allowing the power components ample time to cool, but this time
throttle was increased at a slower rate to gauge the thermal performance. At time of testing, inadequate
thermal contact was made between the ESC and associated water block. The testing was performed as a
worst-case scenario in terms of thermal contact, and the thermal contact issues have since been remedied.
At time of testing, the motor was able to maintain 15% throttle for approximately 90 seconds before the
thermal limits of the equipment were reached. Corrective measures were taken to ensure better thermal
contact between heat generating components and water block.
The test illustrated the durability of the materials used in the propellers and shaft, demonstrating
that these would likely not be points of failure under operation. Additionally, the ability of the power
system to perform for an extended period without overheating with inadequate cooling bolstered
confidence in the effectiveness of the cooling system as it stands. Additionally, the strain data gained
during the test allowed a thrust to throttle percentage curve to be determined, allowing the potential thrust
of the system at different currents to be estimated. The height of the test rig was also varied during 22
operation to mitigate propeller cavitation, giving valuable insight into the height at which the propellers
should be mounted relative to the surface of the water.
These tests will be repeated following the retrofitting of the power system with more robust
components, including cast aluminum propellers and a more rigorous thermal management system. Future
testing will take place with the propulsion system fully packaged inside the finished boat to determine the
boat’s dynamic properties, as well as to determine the limits to be set in the control system relating to
power delivery and calibration. 23
Risks
During the design and build process, we identified and mitigated key risks to enhance the
reliability and performance of our unmanned vessel. To address potential overheating—an issue that
challenged last year’s team—we developed a robust cooling system incorporating two pumps to actively
cool the electronic speed controllers (ESCs) and motors. Additionally, we applied thermal paste and
installed a cooling block along the ESCs for improved heat dissipation. If overheating persists during
testing, we have contingency plans, including integrating a cooled payload to maintain a lower internal
temperature during the race. To prevent structural failures, we conducted multiple leak tests and
reinforced high-risk areas—primarily in the rear of the vessel—with additional material layers. These
areas were patched, tested, and sealed for durability. Weight was a critical design consideration; we used
SolidWorks to estimate total mass and ANSYS simulations to validate the vessel’s structural integrity
under load conditions. To mitigate battery failure risks, we procured extra batteries and implemented a
structured charging schedule leading up to the race. We also maximized the number of parallel battery
connections to reduce current draw per cell, enhancing overall power efficiency. Additionally, to protect
the vessel during transit, we invested in a trailer and constructed a custom stand for secure transportation.
As race day approaches, we will continue monitoring heat levels, battery performance, and
structural integrity in real time, ensuring optimal performance while proactively addressing emerging
risks.24

Figure (10). Catamaran Hull Design
Catamarans offer fantastic stability and lift characteristics. However, the tunnel in the center of the
boat induces lots of stress onto the frame of the boat.
Figure (11). Mono-hull Design
Mono-hull designs are great at planing on top of the water, storing equipment internally, and are
highly maneuverable. Most importantly, this design is easy to manufacture.27
Figure (12). Tri-hull Design

Tri-hulls aim to balance the maneuverability of a mono-hull with the stability of a catamaran. Trihulls are just “ok” at these features, and the complications that would arise in manufacturing don’t make
them worth consideration.
